# Infant Solid Foods Mixed

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="infant-solid-foods-mixed-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="infant-solid-foods-mixed-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="infant-solid-foods-mixed-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Infant Solid Foods Mixed in the HMI library has 989 reported results for lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, monomethylarsonic acid, total mercury, methylmercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, As, AsIII, AsV, B, Ba, Ca, Ga, Hg, K, Li, Mg, Mo, Na and Sr from 22 sources.<sup <li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Infant Solid Foods Mixed, as sold from all stages had total mercury higher at 0.34 µg/kg, against 0.085 µg/kg for Baby food stage 1, 5-6 months in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tatsuta N, Asato K, Iwai-Shimada M, Iwai K, Nakayama SF, Yamazaki S, Nakai K · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Dietary intake of methylmercury by 0–5 years children using the duplicate diet method in Japan</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask for lot results with a quantification limit well below the limit that applies in the destination market.<sup class="cite">[[sources/amarh2023-ghana-infant-food-heavy-metals|1]]<span Infant Solid Foods Mixed, as sold from all stages had total mercury higher at 0.34 µg/kg, against 0.085 µg/kg for Baby food stage 1, 5-6 months in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tatsuta N, Asato K, Iwai-Shimada M, Iwai K, Nakayama SF, Yamazaki S, Nakai K · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Dietary intake of methylmercury by 0–5 years children using the duplicate diet method in Japan</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

For a buyer the practical points are the form bought, the basis a result is reported on, where the infant Solid Foods Mixed came from and the laboratory’s reporting limit. Testing finds contamination but does not remove it.

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-infant-solid-foods-mixed-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one form of infant solid foods mixed, group and metal; percentiles, ranges and maxima reported for the same samples as a mean or median are shown on that row. Different forms and preparation states are kept apart, and dry-weight results never share a reference with as-sold or fresh-weight results. Ratings place a result against an HMI reference built from monitoring results and ordinary-setting medians for the same form and basis. Same-study contrasts compare a contaminated or treated site with its control, targeted with random sampling, a prepared form with the unprocessed one, or one group of a study with the median of its other groups. Held rows failed a check against their own source and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>De et al. 2017</td><td>1</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Rahati et al. 2026</td><td>4</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Sipahi et al. 2014</td><td>1</td><td>25%</td></tr><tr><td>Spungen et al. 2024</td><td>5</td><td>25%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for infant solid foods mixed, as sold on a as sold, as eaten or fresh weight basis: monitoring results summarized as one median per reporting region, sampling type and collection year, total diet composites and printed sample values as single observations, and printed subgroup medians from ordinary farms or markets. Each sampling family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1 to Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>4 sampling families with different designs; none is a probability sample of world supply. Reporting regions and purchase markets are not growing areas. Non-detects with differing limits widen the bounds. <a id="ingredients-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How metals reach infant Solid Foods Mixed

<a id="hmi-prd-010"></a>
<a id="which-ingredients-or-inputs-are-plausible-contributors-and-which-contributions-have-been-measured"></a>
<a id="hmi-prd-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-may-enter-during-manufacturing-handling-or-contact-with-equipment-and-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-prd-012"></a>
<a id="how-do-formulation-ingredient-origins-and-product-format-alter-those-pathways"></a>

The evidence on how metals reach infant Solid Foods Mixed comes from studies that compared exposed and ordinary settings. Infant Solid Foods Mixed, as sold from all stages had total mercury higher at 0.34 µg/kg, against 0.085 µg/kg for Baby food stage 1, 5-6 months in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tatsuta N, Asato K, Iwai-Shimada M, Iwai K, Nakayama SF, Yamazaki S, Nakai K · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Dietary intake of methylmercury by 0–5 years children using the duplicate diet method in Japan</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, infant Solid Foods Mixed, as sold from labelled organic farming had nickel higher at 54.7 µg/kg, against 40.4 µg/kg for all 85 samples in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/pereira2020-nickel-premade-baby-foods|11]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Pereira AMPT, Silva LJG, Simões BDF, Lino C, Pena A · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/pereira2020-nickel-premade-baby-foods">Exposure to nickel through commercial premade baby foods: Is there any risk?</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Food Composition and Analysis</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/pereira2020-nickel-premade-baby-foods">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

These are observational comparisons from single studies; the size of the difference depends on the site, metal and distance.



<a id="manufacturing-packaging-and-storage"></a>
## Manufacturing, packaging and storage

<a id="hmi-prd-013"></a>
<a id="how-do-manufacturing-and-preparation-change-concentrations-species-or-contaminant-mass"></a>
<a id="hmi-prd-014"></a>
<a id="what-migration-or-release-from-equipment-or-packaging-has-been-measured-under-relevant-conditions"></a>
<a id="hmi-prd-015"></a>
<a id="how-do-storage-duration-temperature-reuse-or-other-use-conditions-affect-contamination"></a>

Processed or prepared forms were compared only with unprocessed infant Solid Foods Mixed in the same study and group. Infant Solid Foods Mixed, flour or meal (Mixtures) had lead lower at 1.4 µg/kg, against 1.6 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (infant solid foods mixed, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Analytical Results for Lead in Food Intended for Babies and Young Children (FY2020-FY2021)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA analytical results table</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, infant Solid Foods Mixed, flour or meal (Mixtures) had lead lower at 1.9 µg/kg, against 2.6 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (infant solid foods mixed, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2024-lead-baby-food-fy2023-guidance-basis|13]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2024-lead-baby-food-fy2023-guidance-basis">Analytical Results for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children (FY2023)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA analytical results table</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2024-lead-baby-food-fy2023-guidance-basis">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Forms differ in water content, so a per-kilogram difference is not by itself a measured removal or gain of metal.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Infant Solid Foods Mixed FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-are-found-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-question="What heavy metals are found in infant Solid Foods Mixed?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals are found in infant Solid Foods Mixed?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

The library reports lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic, dimethylarsinic acid, monomethylarsonic acid, total mercury, methylmercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin, antimony, Co, Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, V, Se, As, AsIII, AsV, B, Ba, Ca, Ga, Hg, K, Li, Mg, Mo, Na and Sr in infant Solid Foods Mixed, most often lead, cadmium and total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/amarh2023-ghana-infant-food-heavy-metals|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Flora Amerley Amarh, Eric Selorm Agorku, Ray <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-question="How do heavy metals get into infant Solid Foods Mixed?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into infant Solid Foods Mixed?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In the studies available, infant Solid Foods Mixed from contaminated or exposed settings carried more metal than infant Solid Foods Mixed from the same study’s control.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tatsuta N, Asato K, Iwai-Shimada M, Iwai K, Nakayama SF, Yamazaki S, Nakai K · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Dietary intake of methylmercury by 0–5 years children using the duplicate diet method in Japan</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Infant Solid Foods Mixed, as sold from all stages had total mercury higher at 0.34 µg/kg, against 0.085 µg/kg for Baby food stage 1, 5-6 months in the same study.<sup class="cite">[[sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Tatsuta N, Asato K, Iwai-Shimada M, Iwai K, Nakayama SF, Yamazaki S, Nakai K · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Dietary intake of methylmercury by 0–5 years children using the duplicate diet method in Japan</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/tatsuta2024-mehg-duplicate-diet-children-japan">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-origins-or-products-of-infant-solid-foods-mixed-measured-lowest" data-anchor="which-origins-or-products-of-infant-solid-foods-mixed-measured-lowest" data-question="Which origins or products of infant Solid Foods Mixed measured lowest?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which origins or products of infant Solid Foods Mixed measured lowest?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In one study, lead across 22 groups of infant Solid Foods Mixed ranged from 61 µg/kg (retail product PMV, Wa Municipality) to 368 µg/kg (retail product PYP, Wa Municipality); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/amarh2023-ghana-infant-food-heavy-metals|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Flora Amerley Amarh, Eric Selorm Agorku, Ray Bright Voegborlo, Gerheart Winfred Ashong, George Atiah Atongo · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/amarh2023-ghana-infant-food-heavy-metals">Health risk assessment of some selected heavy metals in infant food sold in Wa, Ghana</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Heliyon</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/amarh2023-ghana-infant-food-heavy-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In another study, cadmium across 4 groups of infant Solid Foods Mixed ranged from 7.2 µg/kg (National basket, Slovakia) to 21.8 µg/kg (National basket, Sweden); the lowest is the lowest observed in that study, not an established sourcing preference.<sup class="cite">[[sources/pandelova2012-eu-baby-food-formula-elements|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Pandelova M, Levy Lopez W, Michalke B, Schramm KW · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/pandelova2012-eu-baby-food-formula-elements">Ca, Cd, Cu, Fe, Hg, Mn, Ni, Pb, Se, and Zn contents in baby foods from the EU market: Comparison of assessed infant intakes with the present safety limits for minerals and trace elements</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Journal of Food Composition and Analysis</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/pandelova2012-eu-baby-food-formula-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-anchor="does-processing-change-heavy-metals-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed" data-question="Does processing change heavy metals in infant Solid Foods Mixed?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Does processing change heavy metals in infant Solid Foods Mixed?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Only comparisons between forms in the same study are available, not before-and-after measurements of the same infant Solid Foods Mixed.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Analytical Results for Lead in Food Intended for Babies and Young Children (FY2020-FY2021)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA analytical results table</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Infant Solid Foods Mixed, flour or meal (Mixtures) had lead lower at 1.4 µg/kg, against 1.6 µg/kg for the unprocessed form in the same group (infant solid foods mixed, as sold).<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021|12]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Analytical Results for Lead in Food Intended for Babies and Young Children (FY2020-FY2021)</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA analytical results table</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2021-lead-baby-food-fy2020-fy2021">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed-is-inorganic" data-anchor="how-much-of-the-arsenic-in-infant-solid-foods-mixed-is-inorganic" data-question="How much of the arsenic in infant Solid Foods Mixed is inorganic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How much of the arsenic in infant Solid Foods Mixed is inorganic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Inorganic arsenic, the more toxic form, was measured in 34 results from 4 sources, far fewer than total arsenic.<sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Z, de Silva S, Reichman SM · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia">Arsenic Concentrations and Dietary Exposure in Rice-Based Infant Food in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(2):415</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/guillod-magnin2018-swiss-toddler-rice-arsenic-species|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Guillod-Magnin R, Brüschweiler BJ, Aubert R, Haldimann M · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/guillod-magnin2018-swiss-toddler-rice-arsenic-species">Arsenic species in rice and rice-based products consumed by toddlers in Switzerland</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Food Additives &amp; Contaminants: Part A, 35(6): 1164-1178</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/guillod-magnin2018-swiss-toddler-rice-arsenic-species">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/jackson2012-arsenic-speciation-infant-formulas-first-foods|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Brian P. Jackson, Vivien F. Taylor, Tracy Punshon, Kathryn L. Cottingham · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jackson2012-arsenic-speciation-infant-formulas-first-foods">Arsenic concentration and speciation in infant formulas and first foods</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Pure and Applied Chemistry, Vol. 84, No. 2, pp. 215-223</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jackson2012-arsenic-speciation-infant-formulas-first-foods">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2021-chronic-exposure-iAs|18]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA, Arcella D, Cascio C, Gómez Ruiz JA · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa2021-chronic-exposure-iAs">Chronic dietary exposure to inorganic arsenic</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa2021-chronic-exposure-iAs">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Across 2 other studies of ordinary farms and markets, reported inorganic arsenic means and medians on an as-sold or fresh-weight basis ranged from 8.6 µg/kg (Guillod-Magnin et al. 2018) to 155 µg/kg (Gu et al. 2020).<sup class="cite">[[sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Gu Z, de Silva S, Reichman SM · 2020</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia">Arsenic Concentrations and Dietary Exposure in Rice-Based Infant Food in Australia</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health 17(2):415</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/gu2020-arsenic-rice-infant-food-australia">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/guillod-magnin2018-swiss-toddler-rice-arsenic-species|17]]<span
